the predictions around the Jensen saga were a great demo of how little correlation there is between confidence and being right.

it’s wild how many prominent VCs, analysts and experts spoke with complete confidence about how things would play out .

some flip-flopped on their predictions within days - each time with the same confidence!

our info ecosystem asymmetrically rewards certainty, speed and brashness… “I don’t know,
let’s see how this plays out” just doesn’t get eyeballs.

worth remembering with ALL “expert” commentary you consume - people often have far less certainty than their tone suggests. they just form a view, stake out a position and say it loudly.

take everything with a sack of salt.

this news cycle was also a good way to calibrate on the people who are consistently loud and wrong.

2124969305674748175.text:
New research from Replit on scaling laws for agent swarms. 

We show that scaling the number of agents can yield dramatic performance gains, but unlike traditional scaling laws, more compute doesn't necessarily translate into better results, and how agents organize themselves matters.

- Given a fixed two-hour window, Opus 5.5 went from a 3.7x speedup on NumPy with one agent to 18.9x with 32 agents.

- GPT-6.2 Astra was the strongest solo agent but exhibited negative scaling beyond 8 agents.

- Models spontaneously developed different organizational structures. Decentralized swarms scaled better than those that relied on centralized coordination.

- The parallelizability of the problem was a strong predictor of swarm performance.

- Interestingly, individual model intelligence is a poor predictor of collective intelligence.

We’re also open-sourcing Optimization-Bench to advance research into this new dimension of inference-time scaling.

https://t.co/RXBU7aM5FE

2125353849057853876.text:
America can build the best frontier models and still lose the global AI race. Which is why Jensen’s return matters far beyond Nvidia.

Governments around the world want sovereign AI: models they can run on their own soil, on their own infrastructure, under their own control.

If American companies won’t meet that demand, Chinese companies will. Countries will start with Chinese models, then adopt Chinese infrastructure and chips. Having the smartest model won’t mean much if most of the world runs on someone else’s stack.

We’ve seen a version of this play out with Huawei. China understood that supplying the world’s telecom infrastructure creates lasting strategic influence. Once a country builds its networks around your equipment, it also builds technical expertise, supplier relationships, and future investment around it. Replacing that equipment becomes expensive and disruptive (the US government is now trying to finance replacement operations but it’s been difficult).

That’s why Jensen’s backing of the American open-model ecosystem is so important. Open models give startups the freedom to compete and give countries a reason to build on American technology.

We need both frontier leadership and global adoption. Open models are essential to getting both. https://t.co/f34FKKbljl

2125089009018040779.text:
This is a pretty key insight. Services businesses are always held back by their ability to deliver outcomes to customers. 

That scaling essentially only could come from headcount, and no matter how much demand you saw, there was always a finite amount of talent you could get for the problem you were going after. Not to mention, the customer generally always wants the work done faster, at a lower price, or at a higher quality.

Agents entirely change the calculus here, because now we can scale output in a way that’s decoupled from the among of time that goes in. A single engineer can have the output of dozens of engineers before. A single designer can probably build out your entire design system and brand. And so on.

Well why isn’t this just all agents then? Because the key is to still have experts on the front end that actually can ensure the right outcomes are delivered from agents.

It’s likely that we’re going to see this in a wide variety of categories. You’ll see this in cyber security, advertising and marketing, legal, accounting, IT transformation, and a number of other historically people-only services industries.

It’s a great time if you’re starting one of these businesses, or if you have the capability to transform an existing one.

2125442246543814686.text:
This wouldn’t have sounded possible a year ago, but it’s becoming much more reasonable now that you can get 10X output gains based on the latest in AI model and harness progress. The result is that teams within the same company are driving very different levels of output based on how they’ve adopted AI.

This is a different phenomenon from other tech. Typically in the economy you think of technology adoption rates on a per firm basis, because the company generally adopts a relatively standardized approach to doing the new tech thing. Like “that company has gone digital or adopted the cloud”. So generally the uplift across teams is more or less the same across teams. 

AI is starting to look quite different. Even within the same company you can have a 10X delta between the lowest and highest adopters of AI and the impact they’re seeing. The teams that are able to actually figure out how to redesign their processes to best deploy agents in their workflows can see up to an order of magnitude jump in productivity depending on the job function.

Right now this is heavily concentrated in coding, but more work will become coding adjacent so we can expect similar results elsewhere too. This is going to definitely lead to some wild dynamics within companies.

What a year this has been! Time to reflect and do a blog post over the holidays.

OC is in a great place, we found a niche in prosumer and enterprise adoption. The multiplayer team feature is best in class.

Shipping reliable and free open source is also really really hard, and waking up to countless user complaints every day is an emotional challenge. I’m glad the team is taking over most of the work these days.

We mostly been focussing on the boring part of ensuring things are fast, reliable and secure, with the exception of the new memory system and soon OpenClaw ID. 

To many more years!
